title: How force opens a channel
objective: Explain how mechanically gated channels convert membrane force into current.

steps.title: Sensing touch is a physics problem
steps.body:
Light, heat and chemicals carry energy a channel can catch. Force is harder: a touch neuron has to turn a *mechanical* push into an ionic current in under a millisecond.

The answer is **[[mechanically activated channel|mechanically activated channels]]**: ion channels that open when the membrane around them is stretched or deformed.

steps.title: Force-from-lipid, force-from-filament
steps.body:
Two broad ideas for how force reaches the channel:

- **Force-from-lipid:** tension in the membrane itself bends the channel open. [[Piezo2]] works largely this way.
- **Force-from-filament:** the channel is tethered to the cytoskeleton or matrix, and movement pulls it open.

Either way, the gate responds to mechanical stress, not voltage or a ligand.

flag.note: Real endings may combine both mechanisms; details are still being worked out.

visual.alt: A push creates tension in the membrane, which bends a Piezo channel open; cations then flow from outside into the cell.
visual.caption: Membrane tension bends the channel open — force becomes current directly.

options: Because mechanical force itself travels faster than light does
The channel is opened directly by force, with no messenger relay between
It runs through a slow enzyme cascade that then amplifies the signal
It waits for calcium to be released from internal stores first
steps.explanation: Directly mechanically gated channels skip the slow biochemical relays, so touch can be signaled almost instantly, fast enough to adjust grip in real time.

variants.setup: Touch has to be signaled fast enough to adjust your grip as an object starts to slip.
variants.prompt: How does a mechanically gated channel manage that speed?
options: Through a slow amplifying enzyme cascade
Force opens the channel directly, with no messenger relay
By first waiting for calcium from internal stores
By converting the force into light
variants.reveal: Direct mechanical gating skips biochemical relays, so force becomes current almost instantly.

steps.setup: You stretch a patch of membrane containing a mechanically activated channel in a dish, with no other cells around.
options: No; a channel needs a whole animal to show any mechanical response
Yes: if it's intrinsically mechanosensitive, membrane tension alone opens it
Only if capsaicin is added to the patch alongside the applied stretch
Only in darkness, since light would interfere with the recording
steps.reveal: A channel that opens to membrane stretch in an isolated patch is probably intrinsically mechanosensitive. The strongest proof is the purified channel opening in an artificial lipid membrane, later shown for Piezo1 (next lesson).

variants.prompt: You stretch an isolated membrane patch holding a candidate channel and record current. This suggests the channel is…
options: Active only within a whole animal
Intrinsically mechanosensitive — opened by tension itself
variants.explanation: Current from stretch alone, with no other cells or messengers, points to intrinsic mechanosensitivity. The strongest proof is the purified channel opening in an artificial lipid membrane, later shown for Piezo1.
